# Deuteronomy 15: research notes for the verse-by-verse commentary

**How to use these notes:** Every point below comes from a page I actually read, and its link follows it. I ran out of search and fetch requests before I could check some sources. Those gaps are listed at the end.

---

## Section-level notes (vv. 1–11)

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** He says the debt release was meant to keep a permanent underclass from forming in Israel. He also notes that ancient Israel probably never fully practised it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
- **Cambridge Bible (on biblehub):** It calls vv. 7–11 "One of the most beautiful as it is one of the most characteristic passages in the laws of D", partly because the law reaches into the thoughts of the heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-7.htm
- **Whether Israel kept the law:** Precept Austin cites 2 Chronicles 36:21 to say the exile was a result of the Jews' failure to keep this Law. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62497/ The Catholic Encyclopedia agrees that the year was not well observed before the Captivity. It adds that after the return, the people covenanted to let the land lie fallow and to exact no debt in the seventh year (Nehemiah 10:31), and thereafter it was regularly kept. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13289a.htm

---

## Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Ellicott:** This law extends Exodus 21 and Leviticus 25. On top of freeing slaves and resting the land in the seventh year, there was also a release of debts, of which all the Israelites must have the benefit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **The Hebrew word:** The Pulpit Commentary derives "release" (*shemittah*) from a verb meaning to leave or to let lie fallow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-1.htm Precept Austin adds that the same word is used in Exodus 23:10–11 for land lying fallow every seven years. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62497/
- **"At the end":** The ISBE (on netbible.org) warns against reading this too strictly. It means *during* the seventh year, which is naturally identified with the Sabbatical year. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Sabbatical+year

**v. 2: Were debts cancelled for good, or only paused for a year? (a real disagreement)**

This divides individual teachers rather than whole denominations.
- **Cancelled for good:**
  - Guzik mentions the one-year view but thinks it is more likely that it refers to a complete cancellation of debt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
  - Meredith Kline (Reformed) argues the release is permanent, because the seventh year and the Jubilee form one symbolic unit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-15-commentary
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ) says the plain meaning is that all debts to fellow Israelites were cancelled. https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/deuteronomy/15-1.html
- **Paused for a year:**
  - Calvin (Reformed) rejects the idea that debts were wiped out. He argues that God's command to lend even when the seventh year is near would make no sense unless it had been lawful to seek repayment in due time.
  - Constable (evangelical) says the word means "to postpone" rather than "to cancel." The debt was postponed for a year.
  - Both: https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/deuteronomy/15-1.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch take it as simply not pressing for repayment during the seventh year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-1.htm
- **Catholic view:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Talmudists took it as full remission, but modern commentators generally hold that it merely suspended the obligation to pay. It also calls the Douay translation of this verse incorrect. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13289a.htm
- **Jewish practice:** McClintock & Strong's Cyclopedia argues from the later rabbinic *prosbul* (a court declaration that let lenders get round the release) that the release was final. It adds that the teachers of Jesus' day had in effect done away with the law. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/s/sabbatical-year.html
- **"The LORD's release":** Grant stresses that the credit belongs to the Lord, who commanded it, not to the creditor. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62497/

**v. 3**
- **Who the "foreigner" is:**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says this is a foreigner with no settled tie to Israel. That is different from the resident stranger, who could claim their kindness. The rule "breathes no hatred of foreigners". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-3.htm
  - Barnes says the foreigner did not keep the sabbatical year and could earn his usual income that year, so he could still pay. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bbe/deuteronomy/15-1.html
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia makes the same point. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13289a.htm
- **Thompson (quoted by Guzik):** The law was meant to relieve poverty within the covenant community. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
- **Gill (Baptist) reads it as a picture of salvation:** Only those who belong to the Lord (chosen, redeemed and called) receive his forgiveness. "Foreigners" have no share in it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-3.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** He assumes the debtor was a poor Israelite who borrowed to feed his family, not to trade. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm

**v. 4: How to read "there will be no poor among you"**
- **The KJV wording:** The KJV says "Save when." Ellicott, Benson and JFB note the margin reading "to the end that," meaning the law exists so that no one is pushed into poverty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-4.htm
- **Pulpit:** The law was not meant to stop creditors collecting fair debts. It was meant to keep poverty out of the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-4.htm
- **Gill:** The law was never meant to shield rich people from paying their debts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-4.htm
- **Ellicott links it to Acts 4:34**, where no one among the believers was in need. The blessing need not be equal prosperity for all, as long as the well-off remember the poor so that no one is left in want. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Guzik:** God set up a system in which no one *had* to stay poor. God did not unconditionally guarantee prosperity for Israel, either on a national or individual basis. The LORD did guarantee the opportunity for prosperity for an obedient Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**v. 5**
- **Ellicott:** He cites Rashi's reading that if they obey, no one among them will be in want, which matches the spirit of Acts 4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **JFB:** The promised plenty depends on obedience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-4.htm

**v. 6**
- **Ellicott:** He links "as he promised" to the promise to Abram (Genesis 12:2). He notes that the Hebrew root for "lend" is closely tied to the word for "slave," recalling Proverbs 22:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Calvin:** He says "lend to many nations" is said "by way of amplification." So if anyone in Israel was in want, it would be the people's own fault. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/15-6.html
- **Gill:** The promise was fulfilled under David and Solomon, and it lasted only while Israel obeyed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/15-6.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Being able to lend should be seen as a mercy and a reason to do good with what we have. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/15-6.html
- **Modern application:** The Bible Hub Study Bible draws a stewardship lesson ("lending rather than borrowing") and points to Romans 13:8. https://biblehub.com/study/deuteronomy/15-6.htm
- **Prosperity teaching:** I found no prosperity or word-of-faith material on this verse within the permitted sites.

**v. 7**
- **Ellicott, citing Rashi:** The poor of your own city come before the poor of another city. Some people stretch out a hand to give and then close it, which is why the text says both "do not harden" and "do not shut." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Pulpit:** "Harden" literally means to make strong, so as to hold back natural compassion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-7.htm
- **Guzik:** The priority is the needy brother in one's own community. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**v. 8**
- **Ellicott, citing Rashi:** If the poor man won't accept a gift, offer it as a loan. Give enough for his need, though "it is not thy duty to make him rich." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Clarke (via Guzik):** Giving should match the person's distress and your ability to help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**v. 9**
- **Matthew Henry:** God's law governs our thoughts too. He calls it a wicked heart that turns God's command to forgive debts into an excuse not to give. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Guzik:** The release law might discourage *lending*, so God tells them to be generous givers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
- **Precept Austin:** Lending close to the release year meant the lender would get little back, but God told them to lend anyway and promised to bless them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/62497/

**v. 10**
- **Pulpit:** "Grieved" literally means "become evil," that is, hold a grudge. They were to give cheerfully, as in 2 Corinthians 9:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-10.htm
- **Gill:** Lending to someone this poor, with the release year near, amounts to giving. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-10.htm
- **Ellicott, citing Rashi:** Even a promise to give is rewarded. Ellicott compares 2 Corinthians 8:12. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** He says this promises a reward in this life. Against the covetous claim that giving ruins us, he says cheerful giving enriches. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm

**v. 11**
- **Does it contradict v. 4?** Pulpit says no: v. 4 is about *preventing* poverty, and v. 11 is about the *ongoing need* to relieve it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-11.htm
- **Ellicott:** People will always fall into poverty, but it is our business to see that they do not remain in want. The words "thy poor" and "thy needy" mean we cannot shrug off responsibility for any one case. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Poole:** God allows poverty to continue partly as punishment for disobedience and partly to test their charity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-11.htm
- **Kalland and Spurgeon (via Guzik):** Kalland suggests Jesus may have had this verse in mind in "the poor you will always have with you" (Matthew 26:11). Spurgeon notes that God says "thy poor," not "the poor." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
- **Constable:** The verse describes what would actually happen, because Israel would not fully obey. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/15-6.html

**v. 12**
- **Ellicott:** This repeats Exodus 21:2–11 and is cited in Jeremiah 34:9, 13–14. He takes "the seventh year" as the Sabbatical year whenever it fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **A different view:** The Catholic Encyclopedia says this slave law is wrongly connected by some writers with the sabbatical year. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/sabbatical-year
- **Guzik:** These were people who sold themselves into service because of debt. The worst outcome was six years of unpaid work. He sees such servitude as better than the alternative of starving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**vv. 13–14**
- **Ellicott:** Freed servants had to be given the means for a fresh start. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Precept Austin:** After six years a servant had almost nothing of his own, so freedom was to come with a full hand. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-15-commentary
- **Guzik:** The gift also gave the servant hope and a reason to work well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**v. 15**
- **Matthew Henry:** God did not send Israel out of Egypt empty-handed, so they must not send their servants out empty-handed. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Ellicott:** He links this to Leviticus 25:42, where Israelites are God's servants and may not be sold permanently. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **JFB:** It describes this kindness to slaves as unmatched in that era. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-15.htm

**vv. 16–17: The pierced ear**
- **Pulpit:** A servant who wanted to stay was not forced out. The ear-piercing ceremony made him a servant for life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-16.htm
- **Gill, following the Targum:** The door was that of the court, not the master's house. "Forever" meant until the Jubilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-17.htm
- **Precept Austin:** Comparing Exodus, it probably means the servant was brought before the judges. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-15-commentary
- **The maidservant:** Ellicott, citing Rashi, says "likewise" means she too is given gifts, and possibly may stay if she wishes. He says this does not contradict Exodus 21:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Guzik's Christ-centred reading:** The pierced ear shows willing love, and Jesus is the great fulfillment of this willing slave. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/
- **Matthew Henry:** Some may have thought such a servant mean-spirited, while others respected his contented, loyal spirit. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm

**v. 18**
- **Matthew Henry:** A hired worker served at most three years (Isaiah 16:14). This servant gave six years with no wages. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** Translations differ on the "double" wording. It notes that the blessing is again tied to obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-15-commentary
- **Constable:** The blessing-for-obedience promise appears four times in the chapter (vv. 4, 6, 10, 18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/15-6.html

**v. 19**
- **Ellicott:** To "sanctify" the firstborn means to treat them as the Lord's property by not using them for ordinary work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** This recalls the sparing of Israel's firstborn in Egypt. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Precept Austin:** The firstborn were to bring no benefit to their owners. https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-15-commentary
- **Guzik:** The point is not that God loves only the perfect. Real sacrifice means giving what is most valuable to us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-15/

**v. 20**
- **Ellicott:** He connects this to the second tithe (Deuteronomy 14:23). He admits it is hard to square with Numbers 18:15, which gives the firstborn to the priests. He lists Rashi's view that "you shall eat" refers to the priest, and his own preferred solution of separate collections at different times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm

**v. 21**
- **Matthew Henry:** A blemished animal was unfit to honour God or to picture Christ, the Lamb without blemish. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The general sacrifice rules already covered this, but it was still important to apply them to the firstborn specifically. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-22.htm

**v. 22**
- **Gill:** A blemished firstborn could be eaten as ordinary food at home. Even those who were ceremonially unclean could eat it, just like gazelle or deer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/15-22.htm
- **Bible Hub Study Bible:** It sees a foreshadowing of Acts 10:15. https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/15-22.htm

**v. 23**
- **Matthew Henry:** Repeating the ban on blood shows how much weight God put on it. He adds that Christians are not under this yoke but should apply its gospel meaning by giving God the first of their time and strength. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
- **Clarke:** Game such as deer was often shot with arrows, so its blood could not be poured out at the altar. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/deuteronomy/12-15.html

---

## Other views

- **Christ-centred and gospel readings:**
  - Matthew Henry: the year of release typified the grace of the gospel, pictures the forgiveness of sins, and teaches us to forgive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Deu/Deu_015.cfm
  - Trapp: it signified the kingdom of Christ, linked to Matthew 6:12. https://www.studylight.org/bible/heb/hmd/deuteronomy/15-1.html
- **Catholic:** In *Tertio Millennio Adveniente* (1994), John Paul II places the sabbatical year (fallow land, freed slaves, cancelled debts) within the jubilee tradition. He says Jesus' words and deeds fulfil that tradition. https://www.newadvent.org/library/docs_jp02tm.htm
- **Jewish interpretation:** Ellicott draws heavily on Rashi for vv. 7–10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/15.htm The Pulpit Commentary says rabbinic tradition effectively cancelled the debt-release law. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-25.html

## What I couldn't find

- Comments specific to this chapter from Methodist (Wesley), Pentecostal, Lutheran, Anglican, or Orthodox (oca.org) teachers.
- NET Bible translator notes, apart from one short note quoted on Precept Austin about v. 22.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.

The Protestant disagreements I did find (debt cancelled vs. paused, and how to read v. 4) are between individual teachers. I found no evidence that they follow denominational lines.
